screens.title: User account lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: A user account is a named identity on a system that associates a username with a UID, a primary group, optional supplementary groups, a login shell, and a home directory. Practically, an account gives a person or a service a namespace and ownership for files, and authentication credentials so that access control systems and audits can tie actions to identities. The lifecycle starts when you create an account with a command like useradd. Creating it with the right options—home directory, shell, and groups—ensures the account is usable and has the expected environment. Next, the account may need changes: passwords rotated with passwd, shells or homes updated with usermod, and group memberships adjusted. Finally, when access is no longer needed, the account is removed with userdel, either preserving files for audit or removing them with the -r option. An example: creating a developer account that needs a bash shell, a home directory, and membership in a developers group keeps their files organized under /home and allows consistent shell behavior. A common misconception is that user creation is harmless; in fact, missing the -m option or forgetting to set a password can leave the account unusable or inconsistent with policy. The core takeaway is to treat each lifecycle stage as a policy decision—create deliberately, modify safely, and delete with a data-retention plan.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › User account lifecycle
Definition

A user account maps identity to UID, groups, home, and shell, and it controls file ownership and login capability.

Create
useradd with options to set home, shell, and groups.
Modify
usermod to move home, change shell, or adjust groups.
Remove
userdel with optional -r to remove home and mail spools.
Operational stages
Stage 1
Provision account with useradd, include -m to create a usable home.
Stage 2
Set a password with passwd or lock if the account is for a service.
Stage 3
Adjust attributes using usermod, move home with -m to preserve files.
Stage 4
Retire the account with userdel; choose -r only after backup or policy approval.

screens.title: useradd command and defaults
screens.narratorSegment: The useradd command creates a new user record in system account files. By default it typically writes an entry into /etc/passwd, creates a primary group with the same name, assigns a UID, and sets a default shell and home path such as /home/username. On many distributions a home directory is only created if you add -m, so omitting that flag can leave a user without a usable home directory. For deterministic admin work, supply options explicitly: -m to create the home directory, -d to specify a custom home path, -s to choose a shell, -g to set the primary group, and -G to add supplementary groups. A concrete example: to create devuser with a home, bash shell, primary group developers and supplementary group webteam you would run the long command that includes -m -d -s -g and -G. A common misconception is that defaults are universal across distributions; they are not. Another trap is using -u to assign a UID that conflicts with an existing user. Before you specify a UID, check existing /etc/passwd to avoid reuse. The practical rule: be explicit and verify the account after creation with id and grep in /etc/passwd. What will you check first after creating a user?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › useradd command and defaults
Quick explanation

useradd writes the account record, assigns UID and group, and may create a home depending on flags and distribution defaults.

Verification commands
id username grep username /etc/passwd ls -ld /home/username
Common pitfall
Omitting -m leaves no home created on some systems. Always decide whether you need the home at creation time.
Example
sudo useradd -m -d /home/devuser -s /bin/bash -g developers -G webteam -c "Development User" devuser
Run passwd next to set a login password: sudo passwd devuser. If this account is for a service, set the shell to /sbin/nologin and lock the password instead.
Tip: Always verify with id and /etc/passwd after creation.

screens.title: Setting passwords and locking accounts
screens.narratorSegment: Passwords are set and managed with the passwd command. For an interactive user you will run passwd after creating the account and supply a strong, unique password when prompted. This ties the account to password-based authentication handled by PAM. For a service or system account that should not accept interactive logins, the recommended pattern is to set the account's shell to a non-interactive shell such as /sbin/nologin and to lock the password with passwd -l username. Locking places an indicator that prevents password-based authentication while leaving the account available for non-password uses, if any such uses exist. One common misconception is that an account without a password is automatically safe; the reality depends on PAM and other authentication methods. Another trap is setting passwords in scripts without protecting them—avoid plain-text passwords in automation. For automation, create a system account (often with -r) and rely on file permissions or key-based mechanisms for service authentication. Example commands are shown in the code panel; after any password or lock operation verify with su - username or id to confirm behavior. The key takeaway: choose the right authentication method for the account's role and verify the effect immediately.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Setting passwords and locking accounts
Interactive account flow
sudo passwd testuser1
# Enter a strong password when prompted

After setting the password, verify you can switch user or authenticate over SSH if allowed. Use strong, unique passwords and rotate them per policy.

Service account pattern
sudo useradd -r -d /var/www/webapp -s /sbin/nologin -G www-data -c "Web Application Service User" webapp
sudo passwd -l webapp

This prevents password-based logins. Use -r to create a system account and lock the password if the service does not require an interactive session.

Check: su - webapp should fail due to nologin or locked password.

screens.title: Modifying accounts with usermod
screens.narratorSegment: usermod changes attributes for an existing user and must be used with intent. A core use is changing a user's home directory while preserving files. Use usermod -d /new/home/username -m username to update the passwd entry and move the existing files; the -m is essential because without it you change the record but leave the files behind. If you need to change a username, usermod -l newname oldname replaces the login while keeping the UID and other attributes. Changing supplementary groups requires care: use usermod -aG group username to append the new group. Omitting -a will replace the supplementary group list and remove the user from groups they should keep, which is a frequent operational mistake. To change the primary group use -g, and to change the login shell use -s /bin/zsh. When moving home directories, check file ownership afterwards and update SELinux contexts or service references if applicable. A concrete scenario: moving alice's home to /srv/alice while preserving files uses -d and -m, then run id and ls -ld to verify ownership. The takeaway: usermod is powerful and destructive if flags are misused—double-check the flags and verify the system state after each change.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Modifying accounts with usermod
Key commands and their meaning
Move home and update record: 
sudo usermod -d /new/home/devuser -m devuser
Change shell: 
sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh username
Change username: 
sudo usermod -l newname oldname
Group membership example and warning
# Correct: append new group
sudo usermod -aG qa developer

# Incorrect: replaces existing supplementary groups
sudo usermod -G qa developer
Verify with id developer to see the full list of groups after the change. If you accidentally replaced groups, restore them from /etc/group or a backup.

screens.title: Appending vs replacing supplementary groups
screens.narratorSegment: Supplementary groups give users extra permissions for shared resources. The usermod -G option sets the user's supplementary group list, but its behavior depends on whether you also use -a. If you run usermod -G group user without -a, it replaces the user's entire supplementary group list with the specified group. That can inadvertently remove the user from groups they still need. By contrast, usermod -aG group user appends the new group to the existing list, preserving current memberships. A concrete example: a developer who is already in groups devs and testers needs QA access. Running usermod -G qa developer will remove devs and testers and leave only qa. Running usermod -aG qa developer preserves devs and testers and adds qa. The common misconception is that -G always appends; it does not. Always use -a when your intent is to add a group. To verify, run id username after the change to confirm the expected memberships. If you accidentally remove groups, restore them manually or from a backup. The practical rule: if you cannot confidently list all current supplementary groups, use -a to append and avoid destructive changes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Appending vs replacing supplementary groups
Scenario

Developer is in groups devs and testers. You need to add them to qa without removing existing groups.

Correct: append
sudo usermod -aG qa developer
id developer
Incorrect: replace
sudo usermod -G qa developer
id developer
Check and recover

If groups were replaced accidentally, inspect /etc/group and re-add missing memberships or restore from backups. Keep an audit log of group changes when possible.

Tip: run id before and after changes to confirm the delta.

screens.title: Changing a user's home directory safely
screens.narratorSegment: Moving a user's home directory is a common administrative need when storage or organizational structure changes. The safe way to do this is using usermod -d newpath username together with -m. The -d updates the path stored in /etc/passwd, and -m moves the files from the old home to the new location. Without -m you only update the record and leave files where they were, causing a broken environment at next login. After the move you must verify file ownership and permissions with ls -ld and find commands, and fix ownership if necessary using chown -R username:group /newpath. A concrete example: moving alice from /home/alice to /srv/alice uses sudo usermod -d /srv/alice -m alice, then sudo ls -ld /srv/alice and id alice to confirm the UID. Also consider service references, scheduled jobs, or SELinux context changes that might still point to the old path. A misconception is that usermod will automatically update every path on the system; it only changes account records and the files moved with -m. The takeaway: when moving homes, include -m, verify ownership, and update any external references.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Changing a user's home directory safely
Command example
sudo usermod -d /srv/alice -m alice
ls -ld /srv/alice
id alice

If ownership is wrong, fix with chown -R alice:alice /srv/alice. Then test login or su to ensure the environment loads correctly.

Checklist
  • Include -m when moving home to move files.
  • Verify file ownership and permissions.
  • Update external references like cron or service configs.
Pro tip: back up the old home before moving if audits require retention.

screens.title: Service accounts and system users
screens.narratorSegment: Service accounts are non-interactive accounts used by applications or system services. They usually do not require a login shell or a human password. The recommended approach is to create them as system accounts when appropriate and to choose a non-login shell to prevent interactive sessions. The useradd -r option creates a system account with a UID from the system range and is commonly used for service accounts. Additionally, set the shell to /sbin/nologin and lock the password with passwd -l to make sure no one can authenticate using a password for that account. For example, create a webapp account whose files live under /var/www/webapp, belong to the www-data group, and cannot be used for a login session. A misconception is that a locked password means the service cannot use the account; many services run as that user without requiring password authentication. Finally, avoid setting an interactive shell or leaving a usable password on a service account. The practical benefit of these patterns is to minimize attack surface and separate human user accounts from service identities. Service accounts and system users means use system accounts, non-interactive shells, and locked passwords for services to reduce attack surface and avoid accidental logins.. In practical terms, when to create a system account and how to disable interactive login. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Deleting accounts and handling data
screens.narratorSegment: Deleting a user account is an irreversible operational step unless you have a backup. The userdel command removes the account entry from system files. By default it leaves the home directory and mail spool intact so administrators can audit or recover data. If policy or cleanup requires removing the home and mail, use userdel -r username to remove the account and its home directory. Before deleting, always check for files owned by the UID outside the home directory using find / -uid UID -exec ls -ld {} \; so you don't leave orphaned files. Also decide whether to archive the home directory first. A common mistake is running userdel -r without backing up user data that will be needed for compliance or handover. Another risk is reusing the UID immediately after deletion; wait or reserve the UID to avoid ownership confusion. Walkthrough: check id username to learn the UID, find files by UID, create an archive with tar if needed, then run userdel -r if policy allows. The key takeaway: deletion must follow a documented retention or archival step to avoid data loss and maintain auditability.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Deleting accounts and handling data
Checklist before deletion
  • Check UID and current file ownerships with id and find.
  • Archive or transfer needed files from the home directory.
  • Decide whether policy allows removal with -r or requires retention.
Example removal flow
# Find files owned by UID
sudo id devuser
sudo find / -uid 1001 -exec ls -ld {} \;

# Archive home, then remove
sudo tar -czf /archives/devuser-home.tar.gz /home/devuser
sudo userdel -r devuser
Reminder: back up first if any forensic or business records are required.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: Many account management incidents come from a handful of small mistakes. Forgetting to set a password leaves a newly created account unusable until you set one or explicitly lock it for a service. Running usermod -G without -a replaces supplementary groups and can silently remove important access rights. Moving a home directory without -m updates only the record and leaves files behind, creating a broken environment at login. Deleting an account without backing up or archiving the home directory can permanently remove business-critical data. Reusing UIDs later can misattribute file ownership to a different person. The safety practices are straightforward: always be explicit with flags, verify each change with id, grep /etc/passwd, and ls -ld, run find by UID when deleting accounts, and maintain simple backups or archives for deletions. Additionally, document changes in an audit log so you can recover memberships or file ownership if needed. A small checklist before any change—verify flags, check current groups, back up data—prevents most incidents. The key insight is that predictable commands, concise verification, and a small dose of caution makes user management low-risk and auditable.

screens.title: User Account Lifecycle: lab walkthrough

fullNarratorScript:
Managing local user accounts is a core administrative responsibility that determines who can access a system and how. In this lesson you will learn the lifecycle tasks: creating accounts with appropriate home directories and shells, setting secure passwords or locking accounts, modifying attributes when roles change, and safely removing accounts and their data. You'll also learn the precise command options and the small mistakes that cause big problems, like overwriting supplementary groups or leaving orphaned home directories. Practical examples will show a full user creation workflow, how to change a home directory while preserving files, how to add a user to groups without removing existing memberships, and how to delete an account with or without its data depending on policy. By the end you will understand both the commands and the reasoning behind each option so you can make choices that match security and operational needs. Keep an eye out for the common pitfalls: forgetting to set a password, using the wrong usermod flags, or unintentionally reusing UIDs. Ready to explore the core commands and safe patterns that make user management predictable and auditable?

By the end of these screens you will be able to perform the core actions of user lifecycle management and explain why each choice matters. You will create accounts with specific home directories and shells, assign primary and supplementary groups correctly, and apply secure password handling and account locking. You will also practice modifying a user's attributes without breaking access, including moving home directories and changing login shells. Finally, you will delete accounts deliberately, deciding whether to remove or archive home data and understanding the audit and security implications. Each objective links a concrete command to the real operational choice it supports. For example, using the -m flag creates a home directory so files are available immediately; using usermod -m moves files so the user environment stays intact. You'll practice appending groups safely with -a to avoid accidentally removing existing group memberships, a common pitfall. These are practical competencies you can verify in a lab or during a system audit. Which of these skills would you like to test first?

These additional objectives focus on nuance and safety. You will learn to manage supplementary groups correctly, using append mode so you don't unintentionally remove existing memberships. You will understand UID assignment and why reusing UIDs can cause ownership confusion. You'll practice configuring non-interactive service accounts by setting an appropriate shell and optionally making them system accounts, then locking them if passwords aren't required. Finally, you will learn to identify and avoid the most common mistakes, such as forgetting to move files when changing home directories or using usermod -G without -a. Each objective includes a compact verification step you can run in a terminal to confirm the expected system state. These checks make your changes auditable and reduce accidental downtime. Which safety check will you try first when you practice?

A user account is a named identity on a system that associates a username with a UID, a primary group, optional supplementary groups, a login shell, and a home directory. Practically, an account gives a person or a service a namespace and ownership for files, and authentication credentials so that access control systems and audits can tie actions to identities. The lifecycle starts when you create an account with a command like useradd. Creating it with the right options—home directory, shell, and groups—ensures the account is usable and has the expected environment. Next, the account may need changes: passwords rotated with passwd, shells or homes updated with usermod, and group memberships adjusted. Finally, when access is no longer needed, the account is removed with userdel, either preserving files for audit or removing them with the -r option. An example: creating a developer account that needs a bash shell, a home directory, and membership in a developers group keeps their files organized under /home and allows consistent shell behavior. A common misconception is that user creation is harmless; in fact, missing the -m option or forgetting to set a password can leave the account unusable or inconsistent with policy. The core takeaway is to treat each lifecycle stage as a policy decision—create deliberately, modify safely, and delete with a data-retention plan.

The useradd command creates a new user record in system account files. By default it typically writes an entry into /etc/passwd, creates a primary group with the same name, assigns a UID, and sets a default shell and home path such as /home/username. On many distributions a home directory is only created if you add -m, so omitting that flag can leave a user without a usable home directory. For deterministic admin work, supply options explicitly: -m to create the home directory, -d to specify a custom home path, -s to choose a shell, -g to set the primary group, and -G to add supplementary groups. A concrete example: to create devuser with a home, bash shell, primary group developers and supplementary group webteam you would run the long command that includes -m -d -s -g and -G. A common misconception is that defaults are universal across distributions; they are not. Another trap is using -u to assign a UID that conflicts with an existing user. Before you specify a UID, check existing /etc/passwd to avoid reuse. The practical rule: be explicit and verify the account after creation with id and grep in /etc/passwd. What will you check first after creating a user?

Passwords are set and managed with the passwd command. For an interactive user you will run passwd after creating the account and supply a strong, unique password when prompted. This ties the account to password-based authentication handled by PAM. For a service or system account that should not accept interactive logins, the recommended pattern is to set the account's shell to a non-interactive shell such as /sbin/nologin and to lock the password with passwd -l username. Locking places an indicator that prevents password-based authentication while leaving the account available for non-password uses, if any such uses exist. One common misconception is that an account without a password is automatically safe; the reality depends on PAM and other authentication methods. Another trap is setting passwords in scripts without protecting them—avoid plain-text passwords in automation. For automation, create a system account (often with -r) and rely on file permissions or key-based mechanisms for service authentication. Example commands are shown in the code panel; after any password or lock operation verify with su - username or id to confirm behavior. The key takeaway: choose the right authentication method for the account's role and verify the effect immediately.

usermod changes attributes for an existing user and must be used with intent. A core use is changing a user's home directory while preserving files. Use usermod -d /new/home/username -m username to update the passwd entry and move the existing files; the -m is essential because without it you change the record but leave the files behind. If you need to change a username, usermod -l newname oldname replaces the login while keeping the UID and other attributes. Changing supplementary groups requires care: use usermod -aG group username to append the new group. Omitting -a will replace the supplementary group list and remove the user from groups they should keep, which is a frequent operational mistake. To change the primary group use -g, and to change the login shell use -s /bin/zsh. When moving home directories, check file ownership afterwards and update SELinux contexts or service references if applicable. A concrete scenario: moving alice's home to /srv/alice while preserving files uses -d and -m, then run id and ls -ld to verify ownership. The takeaway: usermod is powerful and destructive if flags are misused—double-check the flags and verify the system state after each change.

Supplementary groups give users extra permissions for shared resources. The usermod -G option sets the user's supplementary group list, but its behavior depends on whether you also use -a. If you run usermod -G group user without -a, it replaces the user's entire supplementary group list with the specified group. That can inadvertently remove the user from groups they still need. By contrast, usermod -aG group user appends the new group to the existing list, preserving current memberships. A concrete example: a developer who is already in groups devs and testers needs QA access. Running usermod -G qa developer will remove devs and testers and leave only qa. Running usermod -aG qa developer preserves devs and testers and adds qa. The common misconception is that -G always appends; it does not. Always use -a when your intent is to add a group. To verify, run id username after the change to confirm the expected memberships. If you accidentally remove groups, restore them manually or from a backup. The practical rule: if you cannot confidently list all current supplementary groups, use -a to append and avoid destructive changes.

Moving a user's home directory is a common administrative need when storage or organizational structure changes. The safe way to do this is using usermod -d newpath username together with -m. The -d updates the path stored in /etc/passwd, and -m moves the files from the old home to the new location. Without -m you only update the record and leave files where they were, causing a broken environment at next login. After the move you must verify file ownership and permissions with ls -ld and find commands, and fix ownership if necessary using chown -R username:group /newpath. A concrete example: moving alice from /home/alice to /srv/alice uses sudo usermod -d /srv/alice -m alice, then sudo ls -ld /srv/alice and id alice to confirm the UID. Also consider service references, scheduled jobs, or SELinux context changes that might still point to the old path. A misconception is that usermod will automatically update every path on the system; it only changes account records and the files moved with -m. The takeaway: when moving homes, include -m, verify ownership, and update any external references.

Service accounts are non-interactive accounts used by applications or system services. They usually do not require a login shell or a human password. The recommended approach is to create them as system accounts when appropriate and to choose a non-login shell to prevent interactive sessions. The useradd -r option creates a system account with a UID from the system range and is commonly used for service accounts. Additionally, set the shell to /sbin/nologin and lock the password with passwd -l to make sure no one can authenticate using a password for that account. For example, create a webapp account whose files live under /var/www/webapp, belong to the www-data group, and cannot be used for a login session. A misconception is that a locked password means the service cannot use the account; many services run as that user without requiring password authentication. Finally, avoid setting an interactive shell or leaving a usable password on a service account. The practical benefit of these patterns is to minimize attack surface and separate human user accounts from service identities.
